title: Catherine and Avignon
hookLine: the popes live in France for seventy years; a dyer's daughter urges the pope back to Rome

cards: The bishop of Rome, in this story, doesn't live in Rome. He lives in a great palace in Avignon, a city on the Rhône in southern France, and so did the popes before him, one after another, for many years. Rome waits.
Then letters start arriving at the papal palace from a young woman in Siena. She isn't a nun in a convent, or a noblewoman, or a scholar. Her father dyes cloth for a living.
And she is telling the pope, with great tenderness and no fear at all, to come home.

teach.b: First, the situation. The popes had settled at Avignon, near the French crown, and stayed through a long run of reigns.
To Catherine, and to others in Italy, it looked as if the Church's center had drifted from the city of Peter and Paul. Second, the woman.
Catherine of Siena was a laywoman of the Dominican family, wearing its habit while living at home. Tradition says she learned to read later in life, and much of what she sent out, she dictated.
Her letters went to popes, kings, queens, even captains of hired soldiers. Third, how she spoke to the pope.
She called him, in her Italian, dolce Cristo in terra, sweet Christ on earth.
That's not flattery; it's a title of honor and a weight.
In her letters to Gregory the Eleventh, she tells him again and again to return to Rome, to be a brave man and not a fearful one, and to trust God more than the voices advising delay.
She even traveled to Avignon to tell him in person. Fourth, what happened.

Gregory did go back to Rome. Historians weigh many reasons for his choice. Catherine's voice is one the Church remembers, and Catholics now honor her as a Doctor of the Church and a patron of Italy and of Europe.
Her letters show a way of urging: honor and plain words, sent straight to the one who needed to hear them.

how: Catholics honor Catherine of Siena as a Doctor of the Church and a patron of Italy and Europe; her feast is kept in the spring, and her letters are read for their mix of tenderness and bold counsel to Church leaders.

o: a dyer's daughter who urged the pope home to Rome
a French queen who brought the popes to Avignon
a Sienese nun who ran a convent for noblewomen

games.q: Catherine and Avignon — tap the pairs.

s: she was a laywoman in the Dominican family, living at home and writing to the powerful.
Catherine called the pope sweet Christ on earth
dolce Cristo in terra: honor and a weight at once.
Catherine only wrote; she never went to Avignon
she traveled there to urge Gregory in person.

games.q: you're Catherine. the pope you honor is putting off a hard choice, and his advisers want him to stay. what do you do?
o: complain about him to your friends.
write to him directly, with love, and tell him to come.
say nothing; it isn't your place.
games.why: she writes to Gregory himself, calling him sweet Christ on earth and urging him to be brave and return to Rome. then she goes to tell him in person.

practice: Bring to mind someone you care about who is putting off something they know they should do: a call, an apology, a doctor's visit.
Instead of a lecture, find one sentence with both of Catherine's halves in it, honor for who they are and a plain word about what's next, and turn it over until it's kind and clear.
If you pray, bring that person to God first; if not, just hold them warmly.

wordCard.voice: Catherine. A dyer's daughter from Siena whose loving, fearless letters urged the pope to leave Avignon and return to Rome. Today's word.

orig.note: Italian, written in the Latin alphabet: 'sweet Christ on earth,' Catherine's name for the pope in her letters.

carryVoice: Your line: go back to rome. Love and plain words can travel in the same letter. Day eight hundred twenty-four.
